transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi... um, yeah. I came in because I’ve barely been sleeping since the warehouse inspection. I just lie there in the dark replaying bits of it over and over. Which is so frustrating because I usually sleep great—I actually bought one of those fancy memory foam mattresses a few months ago, the ones you always hear ads for on podcasts? It’s supposed to have this special cooling gel layer, but it doesn't even matter because when I actually do manage to drift off, I just wake up completely sweaty and wide awake. It feels like I’m right back near that blast... And now my expensive sheets are getting ruined, which is a whole other headache because I bought them at this little boutique downtown that just closed, so I can't even replace them if I wanted to, you know? But yeah, the not sleeping is why I'm here.
Can you tell me more about the warehouse inspection? Was there something about that experience that felt traumatic or especially stressful to you?

Well, I was just there for a standard risk assessment. I'm an insurance underwriter, so I do these walk-throughs sometimes to check sprinkler systems and clearance heights and stuff like that. I actually had to wear my good beige blazer that day because I had a client lunch right after, which was so annoying because warehouses are always so incredibly dusty, you know? 

But yeah, I remember being on the floor, and then I remember hearing this massive explosion. It was so loud. And then... I don't know. The next thing I actually remember is just standing outside in the parking lot afterward. I had all this soot on my jacket—that same beige blazer, just totally covered in it. I actually took it to my dry cleaner, Mr. Rossi, and he said he couldn't get the smell out, which is a huge bummer because he's usually a miracle worker. He got a red wine stain out of a silk blouse for me last New Year's, and I thought for sure that shirt was trash. 

But anyway, the weird part is... the part in between hearing the blast and standing outside with the ruined jacket? It's just... blank. Like, completely gone. No matter how hard I try to piece it together, I just can't remember how I actually got out of the building.
Since the explosion, have you found yourself avoiding places, people, or thoughts that remind you of what happened?

Um, yeah, actually. I guess I have been avoiding things. Like, I haven't even been able to look at the file for that warehouse. It's just sitting on my desk under a stack of other folders. And I've been letting all my calls about industrial accounts just go straight to voicemail because even the thought of opening those emails makes my stomach completely drop. Which is so bad for my metrics, honestly. My boss, Greg, is super obsessed with response times. He sends out this weekly spreadsheet color-coded with everyone's average email reply time, and if you're in the red, he makes you have a "quick touch-base" on Friday afternoons. And I hate Friday afternoon meetings, especially now that it's getting warmer and the traffic on I-95 gets so backed up with people heading down to the shore for the weekend. I usually try to leave by 4:00 on Fridays just to beat the worst of it, but Greg always schedules those meetings for 4:30. But yeah, I just can't deal with anything industrial right now, so I'm definitely going to end up in the red this week.
Since the explosion, have you had any sudden, vivid memories or feelings like you’re reliving the event?

Um, yeah, I do. It's really awful. Like, during the day, I’ll just be sitting at my desk reviewing a standard policy or looking at a loss report, and suddenly I get hit with this incredibly sharp image of... of the worker on the floor and all that soot hanging in the air. And it's like my body just reacts before I can even stop it, my heart starts racing and I start sweating. 

Which is actually so embarrassing because our office is open-plan, you know? They did this huge remodel last year to make it more "collaborative," which really just means you have absolutely zero privacy. They even took away the high cubicle walls and replaced them with these tiny frosted glass dividers that don't block anything. And the lighting is so bright—they installed these eco-friendly LED panels that give me a headache by 3 PM. I actually brought in this little Himalayan salt lamp to try and soften the light at my desk, but Brenda from HR said it was a fire hazard, which is ridiculous because she has a space heater under her desk that smells like burning dust every time she turns it on. But yeah, when those images hit me, I feel like everyone in the office can see me panicking, and there's nowhere to hide.
